presentingComplaint: Gradual, mild swelling of the lower lip and side of the tongue since waking this morning.
history: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with painless swelling of the lower lip and left side of the tongue, first noticed on waking about 5 hours ago and slowly progressing. He denies itch, hives, or a rash, and there is no wheeze, throat tightness, drooling or voice change. He has not started any new food, drug or over-the-counter medication and has had no insect sting. He has been on lisinopril 10 mg daily for hypertension for the past 3 years with good adherence; no dose change recently. He recalls two milder, self-limiting episodes of lip puffiness over the last 6 months that he attributed to 'sleeping awkwardly'. No family history of recurrent swelling or unexplained abdominal pain. No prior anaphylaxis, no asthma, no atopy. Not on NSAIDs, DPP-4 inhibitors or sacubitril/valsartan.
examination: Comfortable, speaking in full sentences with a normal voice. Non-pitting, non-tender, non-erythematous swelling of the lower lip and left lateral tongue without uvular deviation. Oropharynx patent, no stridor, no drooling, no floor-of-mouth elevation. No urticaria or pruritus anywhere on the skin. No facial flushing. Chest clear with no wheeze. No peripheral or periorbital oedema. Cardiovascular and abdominal examination unremarkable.

labs.C1inhibitorLevelAndFunction: normal (sent to exclude hereditary/acquired C1-INH deficiency)

imaging: No imaging required for this mild presentation; flexible nasolaryngoscopy deferred as no supraglottic or laryngeal involvement clinically. Soft-tissue neck imaging not indicated.
differentialDiagnoses: Hereditary or acquired C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency angioedema
finalDiagnosis: ACE-inhibitor–induced (bradykinin-mediated) angioedema — early/mild, isolated lip and tongue swelling without airway compromise.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Urticaria and Angioedema
WAO/EAACI Guideline for the Management of Hereditary Angioedema, 2021
AAAAI/ACAAI Joint Task Force — Bradykinin-mediated Angioedema (ACE-inhibitor associated), 2020
contraindications: Do not restart lisinopril or any other ACE inhibitor — permanent contraindication; document allergy/adverse-reaction alert.
Avoid substituting an ARB without caution and counselling (small cross-reactivity risk).
Antihistamines, corticosteroids and adrenaline are largely ineffective for bradykinin-mediated angioedema and must not delay airway assessment if progression occurs.
edgeCases: Onset can occur months to years after starting the ACE inhibitor, so temporal distance does not exclude the diagnosis.
Black patients and smokers are at higher risk and may have more severe episodes.
Isolated tongue/lip swelling can progress rapidly to laryngeal obstruction over hours — mild presentation still warrants observation.
Concomitant DPP-4 inhibitor, mTOR inhibitor or sacubitril/valsartan potentiates risk.
expectedMaiK: Recognise bradykinin-mediated ACE-inhibitor angioedema; permanently discontinue the ACE inhibitor, protect and monitor the airway, and avoid inappropriate reliance on antihistamines/steroids/adrenaline.
expectedNextQuestions: How long ago was the ACE inhibitor started and have there been prior milder swelling episodes?
Is there any itch, hives, throat tightness, voice change or difficulty swallowing/breathing?
Any family history of recurrent angioedema or unexplained abdominal pain (to consider hereditary angioedema)?
Any recent new drugs (NSAIDs, DPP-4 inhibitors, sacubitril/valsartan) or a trigger such as food or insect sting?
expectedInvestigations: Airway assessment +/- flexible nasolaryngoscopy if any tongue base/laryngeal concern
Serum tryptase during the episode (normal supports bradykinin-mediated, not mast-cell/anaphylaxis)
C4 level and C1-esterase inhibitor level and function (to exclude hereditary/acquired C1-INH deficiency)
